hints: Notice the question asks for beta-plus decay, so focus on which nucleon changes and whether an electron or a positron is emitted.
Recall that beta-plus is a proton to neutron conversion, which rules out any option starting neutron to proton with an electron.
Compare the neutral particles in the two remaining proton equations: check whether an electron neutrino or an electron antineutrino balances the lepton number of the emitted positron.
walkthrough: Identify what beta-plus means: in a proton-rich nucleus a proton converts to a neutron and a positron $\beta^+$ is emitted.
Use this to sort the options: options A and B show neutron $\rightarrow$ proton + electron, which is beta-minus decay, so they cannot be beta-plus.
Check charge conservation for the proton change: $+1 \rightarrow 0 + (+1) + 0$, so the proton $\rightarrow$ neutron + positron part needs a neutral neutrino-type particle.
Check lepton number: the positron is an antilepton with lepton number $-1$, so it must be accompanied by a particle with lepton number $+1$ to keep total lepton number zero.
An electron neutrino has electron-lepton number $+1$ while an electron antineutrino has $-1$, so only proton $\rightarrow$ neutron + positron + electron neutrino balances. This is option D

options.A: This is the equation for beta-minus decay, with neutron changing to proton and emitting an electron, not beta-plus decay.
options.B: This starts with neutron to proton and an electron, so it is the wrong nucleon change for beta-plus, and the electron neutrino also breaks lepton number conservation.
options.C: The proton to neutron plus positron part is correct for beta-plus, but the electron antineutrino gives the wrong lepton number balance.
options.D: A proton changes to a neutron with emission of a positron and an electron neutrino, conserving both charge and lepton number for beta-plus decay.
